text: The obstacle in the path becomes the path. Never forget, within every obstacle is an opportunity to improve our condition.
context: His own statement of the book's thesis, written beside the Aurelius line he translates as what stands in the way becoming the way.

text: Wherever you are, whatever you're doing, your worst enemy already lives inside you: your ego.
context: The opening claim of the book, before he defines ego as an unhealthy belief in one's own importance.

text: The ego we see most commonly goes by a more casual definition: an unhealthy belief in our own importance.
context: He sets aside the Freudian sense and uses arrogance and self-centered ambition as the working definition.

text: Ego is the enemy of what you want and of what you have.
context: The sentence that follows the list: craft, insight, other people, loyalty, longevity, and the ability to keep a success.

text: Impressing people is utterly different from being truly impressive.
context: From the John Boyd chapter: rank, title, and the parking space are not the work.

text: Having authority is not the same as being an authority.
context: Paired with the claim that having the right and being right are not the same either.

text: What replaces ego is humility, yes — but rock-hard humility and confidence. Whereas ego is artificial, this type of confidence can hold weight.
context: His distinction: ego is stolen and self-anointed; the confidence that remains is earned.

text: Find canvases for other people to paint on.
context: The apprentice move: clear the path for the people above you, and a path opens for you.

text: That's what the canvas strategy is about — helping yourself by helping others.
context: The strategy has no expiration date. It is available at the start and after success.
Breathlessness, he argues, is a poor substitute for discipline, mastery, and perseverance.

text: To be steady while the world spins around you. To act without frenzy.
context: His English name for the quiet the ancient schools kept describing: apatheia, ataraxia, samatvam, aequanimitas.

text: Stillness is what aims the archer's arrow. It inspires new ideas.
context: From the introduction: stillness sharpens perspective, slows the ball, and makes room for gratitude.

text: This idea of stillness is not some soft New Age nonsense or the domain of monks and sages, but in fact desperately necessary to all of us.
context: He aims the book at people running a fund, playing in a championship, or raising a family, not only at sages.
